title: Falcon Heavy Successfully Launches NASA's Roman Space Telescope
detail: SpaceX's Falcon Heavy lifted off at 7:26 a.m. EDT on August 30, 2026 from Launch Complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center, carrying NASA's $4.3 billion Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. The two side boosters shut down their engines at T+2:24, separated seconds later, and flew boostback burns lasting just over a minute before landing back at Cape Canaveral around T+7:40 — on Landing Zone 2 (the pad's 19th landing) and Landing Zone 40 (the 6th) respectively; the pair had previously flown on the GOES-U and Viasat-3 F3 missions. The center core's engines cut off at T+3:51 ahead of stage separation, and Roman separated cleanly from the Falcon Heavy upper stage at 7:57 a.m. EDT, roughly 31 minutes after liftoff. Roman now begins on-orbit commissioning — deploying its solar array and preparing a mid-course correction burn — on a multi-week transit to the Sun-Earth L2 halo orbit already home to the James Webb Space Telescope, where its 300-megapixel Wide Field Instrument is expected to survey for dark matter and dark energy and could discover roughly 100,000 new exoplanets. The mission was the sixth NASA flagship-class science payload to fly on a SpaceX Falcon rocket from Kennedy and, by tracker tally, SpaceX's 102nd Falcon-family orbital launch of 2026 (exact year-to-date counts vary slightly by source).

title: SpaceX Moves Into Gas-Turbine Manufacturing With New Bastrop, Texas Foundry
detail: Reporting on August 30, 2026 revealed SpaceX is building a foundry to cast blades and vanes for large industrial gas turbines next to its existing Starlink satellite factory in Bastrop, Texas, roughly 30 miles from Austin. SpaceX quietly acquired about 830 acres of surrounding land between March and June 2026, and satellite imagery shows two new buildings that were not present a year earlier. Musk said in-house casting could accelerate delivery of natural-gas turbines — a severely bottlenecked component made at scale by only four companies worldwide, with order backlogs into 2030 — by as much as 18 months, addressing power shortages for AI data centers (including SpaceX's own Starmind AI1 orbital compute ambitions) as well as supplying castings for Raptor engine turbopumps. SpaceX has posted multiple Bastrop job listings for the effort, including senior operations, materials, automation and tooling engineers. The move drew scrutiny from reporters who noted a precedent at Musk's xAI Colossus data center in Memphis, where the NAACP has accused the company of running gas turbines without required permits or pollution controls, and cited a Virginia study estimating that eight turbines at a single site could cause 3.4-6.5 additional premature deaths a year and $53-99 million in annual health costs, with marginalized communities bearing the heaviest exposure — concerns not yet raised specifically against the Bastrop site.

media.caption: SpaceX is building a gas-turbine blade and vane foundry beside its Starlink satellite factory in Bastrop, Texas
